source.title: B ACKDROP : S TOCHASTIC B ACKPROPAGATION

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own interventions and held-out performance outcomes, but evaluates stochastic gradient masking (backdrop), a method not specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports backdrop results on several tasks. No claim version directly covers backdrop; rows are recorded under versions ["none"]. Cited studies of batch size and dropout are not results of this paper.
record.test_reason: The study uses the generalization benefits of stochastic gradients to motivate backdrop and reports its method's performance. Backdrop is not dropout. Although batch sizes are compared, the text does not establish equal epoch budgets, so these comparisons do not test V5's fixed-budget claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that backdrop improves generalization in their non-decomposable-loss and hierarchical-subsample examples, and can lower CIFAR-10 test loss and increase classification confidence. They also acknowledge configuration sensitivity and potentially longer training with very high masking probabilities.
record.recipe_differences: Backdrop stochastically masks gradients during backpropagation while leaving the forward pass intact; it is not a test of the claim's listed interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Mask probability, minibatch size, and masking scale affect reported outcomes; excessive masking can deteriorate generalization in some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Backdrop improves ROC AUC at each tested batch size. At batch size 2048, its improvement exceeds that from reducing the unmasked batch size to 32; batches below 32 perform worse because they poorly approximate the rank statistic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient masking can improve generalization for a non-decomposable ROC AUC objective without reducing the forward-pass batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: Separate gradient masks generally lower test cross-entropy and latent-distance losses. Smaller unmasked minibatches improve the minibatch distance estimate without appreciably improving the full-test distance loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separate backward masks can improve compound-loss optimization when its terms require different sampling scales.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic one-shot textures, the best backdrop configuration reaches 66.2% total accuracy versus 45.9% without masking; stronger masking is not uniformly better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient masking at selected spatial scales can improve generalization on hierarchical textures, with configuration-dependent outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-location 512×512 and 256×256 crops yield 45.3% and 34.3% total accuracy, respectively, below the best backdrop configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cropping can lose useful multiscale information and underperform gradient masking on this synthetic texture task.

fits_no_version.finding: On Ponce textures, increasing backdrop masking improves test accuracy at every tested batch size, with larger gains at larger batches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spatial gradient masking can improve texture classification across batch sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10, backdrop reduces test loss by up to 40%, while accuracy gains are small and sometimes non-significant; excessive masking at small batches can hurt generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdrop can improve held-out cross-entropy more clearly than classification accuracy, with effects depending on masking and batch size.

record.problems: The experiments are presented as demonstrations rather than state-of-the-art comparisons. Several outcomes are reported only in figures without exact values in text; the CIFAR10 accuracy gains are described as small and in some cases not statistically significant. No experiment tests arbitrary-label memorization or the claim's stated mechanisms.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results were omitted. Some figure values are unavailable as text and are recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width beyond the zero-training-error threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning regimes.
Batch-size penalties and their recovery under matched epoch budgets; training budgets are not specified.
Forward-pass dropout, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, not denials of the reported backdrop improvements. The provided text does not preserve readable plotted coordinates, so exact figure values cannot be verified. No additional results directly testing V1–V8 were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same standard training recipe.
Network width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks, sparse local connectivity, and convolutional initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their recovery through recipe changes.
Dropout effects and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removal of memorized training examples and subsequent test accuracy.
